1310.title: The gospel of life (1995)
1310.hook: John Paul II on the value of every human life
1310.howItsDone: Catholics live out the gospel of life through pregnancy and family support, hospice and care for the sick and elderly, outreach to the poor, and advocacy on laws affecting life, and parishes often pray for the protection of life at Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Centesimus Annus: the market as a real good with real edges, and goods that must never be sold. Your line was markets have limits.

In John's Gospel, Jesus talks about sheep, a gate, and a thief. The thief, he says, comes only to steal and to kill and to destroy. Then he gives the opposite reason for his own coming, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am come that they may have life, and may have it more abundantly." Not just kept alive. Abundantly. John Paul the Second wrote a letter that sets life at the center of the gospel, and called it Evangelium Vitae. Today's word is its English name: the gospel of life.
screen: `A THIEF COMES TO DESTROY.` → `I AM COME THAT THEY MAY HAVE LIFE.` → `MORE ABUNDANTLY.`

segments.voice: First, good news, not only a rule. The letter calls the gospel of life the heart of Jesus's message. Life is a gift to be welcomed and helped to grow, before it's a line to defend. Second, an old question. The letter returns to Cain and Abel, where this block heard Cain's dodge. It hears God's question, where is thy brother, asked again wherever a life is ended or treated as worthless, and the dodge coming back too: not my problem. Then God's next words, in the Douay-Rheims: "the voice of thy brother's blood crieth to me from the earth." No life goes unheard. Every life has someone answerable for it. Third, a wide list. Borrowing a list from the Second Vatican Council, the letter gathers many threats to life in one place: murder and genocide, abortion and euthanasia, and also subhuman living conditions, slavery, the selling of women and children, and disgraceful working conditions. The Catholic Church teaches that directly and deliberately taking an innocent human life is always gravely wrong, and the letter applies that teaching to abortion and euthanasia. It also keeps the poor, the sick, the old and the forgotten in the same frame. Fourth, a choice set before everyone. This path heard Moses say it back in year two, in the Douay-Rheims: "Choose therefore life." The letter speaks of building a culture of life: homes, hospitals, laws and habits where the weakest person in the room is safest.
screen: `LIFE AS GOOD NEWS.` · `WHERE IS THY BROTHER?` · `A WIDE LIST OF THREATS.` · then, large: `CHOOSE THEREFORE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Let God's question to Cain become yours: where is my brother, my sister? Bring them to mind one at a time, without hurrying past any: a child not yet born and the mother carrying it, someone in a hospital bed tonight with no visitors, an old neighbor living alone, a person sleeping outside, a worker far away in a dangerous job. If you pray, hold each one before God; if you don't, give each one a breath of real attention.
The gospel of life. John Paul the Second's letter, Evangelium Vitae: every human life a gift, and someone always answerable for it. Today's word.
Your line: every life counts. Not just kept alive, but abundantly. Rest well.

1311.title: The death penalty (CCC 2267)
1311.hook: the Catechism's paragraph 2267 was rewritten to call the death penalty inadmissible
1311.howItsDone: Catholics act on this teaching through prison ministry, visits and letters to people on death row, support for victims' families, and advocacy for the abolition of the death penalty, and bishops' conferences in several countries speak publicly on it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gospel of life: life more abundantly, and a wide list of threats to it. Your line was every life counts.

A few verses after Abel's death in Genesis, Cain, the killer, is afraid: whoever finds him, he says, will kill him. Then something unexpected. In the Douay-Rheims: "And the Lord set a mark upon Cain, that whosoever found him should not kill him." The killer walks away guilty, sent out, and protected. That small mark sits behind a paragraph in the Catechism of the Catholic Church, number 2267, which Pope Francis approved in new words. Today's word is its subject: the death penalty.
screen: `CAIN IS AFRAID.` → `A MARK, SO NO ONE KILLS HIM.` → `PARAGRAPH 2267.`

segments.voice: First, the older wording. The Catechism used to say that the Church's traditional teaching did not rule out the death penalty, if it was the only way to protect people's lives from an unjust aggressor. Drawing on John Paul the Second's gospel of life, it added that cases where that is truly necessary are very rare, if not practically nonexistent. A door left open, but only a crack. Second, the new wording. The revised paragraph says the death penalty is inadmissible, because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person, and that the Church works with determination for its abolition worldwide. Inadmissible: not allowed in, not something the Church can accept. Third, the reasons it gives. A growing awareness that a person's dignity is not lost, even after very serious crimes. A new understanding of what punishment by the state is for. And ways of detaining dangerous people that protect the public without closing off the guilty person's chance to change. John Paul the Second, in yesterday's letter, read Cain's mark the same way: not even a murderer loses his dignity. The Church presents the change as a development of its teaching in the light of the gospel, and Catholic writers have discussed how it fits with what came before. Fourth, the people involved. Jesus in Matthew names among the works that matter, in the Douay-Rheims: "I was in prison, and you came to me." And the Church also keeps close the families of victims, whose grief is real and deserves care. Both are held in the same hands.
screen: `THE OLD WORDING: A DOOR LEFT AJAR.` · `THE NEW WORDING: INADMISSIBLE.` · `DIGNITY ISN'T LOST, EVEN AFTER CRIME.` · then, large: `I WAS IN PRISON, AND YOU CAME TO ME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a prison cell you've never seen, a narrow bed, a small window or none, a person waiting; you don't need to know their crime or decide anything about it, just let them be a person. Then widen the circle: the guards who work there, the chaplain who visits, the families of the people who were harmed, still grieving. If you pray, hold them all before God together; if you don't, hold them in mind without sorting them.
The death penalty. Which the Catechism now calls inadmissible, an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person, even a guilty one. Today's word.
Your line: inadmissible. Even Cain was given a mark of protection. Go gently.

1312.title: Caritas in Veritate (2009)
1312.hook: Benedict XVI: charity in truth, and the place of gift in the economy
1312.howItsDone: Catholics study Caritas in Veritate in parish and university courses on social teaching, and some Catholic business owners point to its logic of gift when shaping how they treat workers and customers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the death penalty, and the Catechism's revised word for it. Your line was inadmissible.

What does a paid-for coffee cost? Most mornings at the counter, everyone ends up square: you pay, they hand you the cup, nobody owes anybody. That's a contract, and it's a fine thing. But some mornings the person ahead of you pays for yours and walks out before you can say anything. Nothing was owed. Nothing can be paid back. Pope Benedict the Sixteenth wrote a letter about the economy, about trade and work and development, and right in the middle of the talk of markets he made room for that second kind of moment.
screen: `A CONTRACT: EVERYONE'S SQUARE.` → `A STRANGER PAYS FOR YOUR COFFEE.` → `GIFT INSIDE THE ECONOMY.`

segments.voice: First, the title. Caritas in veritate is Latin for charity in truth. Caritas is the old Church word for the love that gives itself, the word behind the Douay-Rheims line in the first letter of John: "God is charity." Benedict pairs it with truth on purpose. Love without truth, he warns, slides into sentiment, a warm feeling that can be bent to mean anything. Truth without love turns cold. He wants them held together, the way Paul writes to the Ephesians: "doing the truth in charity." Second, the economy. There's the market, where things are exchanged at an agreed price. There's the state, which shares things out by law. Both, he says, are needed. Neither is enough by itself. Third, the gift. Here's the surprising move. Benedict argues that gratuitousness, giving with no return expected, shouldn't be pushed to the edges, to the charity drive after the real work is done. It should have room within ordinary economic life: in how a business is run, how workers are treated, how a deal is struck. He names this the logic of gift, and roots it in being human: no one made themselves. Every life is received. Fourth, ordinary life. A shift manager who covers for a worker with a sick child. A landlord who doesn't raise the rent on the old tenant. A shop with a pay-it-forward board. None of these break the market. They let something into it that a price can't measure. Jesus says it plainly when he sends out his disciples: "Freely have you received, freely give."
screen: `CHARITY IN TRUTH: HELD TOGETHER.` · `THE MARKET AND THE STATE: NEEDED.` · `GIFT BELONGS INSIDE, NOT AT THE EDGE.` · `WHAT A PRICE CAN'T MEASURE.` · then, large: `FREELY HAVE YOU RECEIVED, FREELY GIVE.`

segments.voice: Picture the people you'll pay tomorrow, the ones who'll serve you, the ones you work beside, and find one moment where you could give something nobody is owed: time, a better tip, a covered shift, a word of thanks with a name in it. Choose one where you won't be thanked, or won't be there to see it. If you pray, offer it to God; if you don't, simply hold the choice quietly.
Caritas in Veritate. Charity in truth: Benedict the Sixteenth's letter on the economy, which makes room for gift alongside contract and law. Today's word.
Your line: the logic of gift. Nothing owed, nothing paid back. That's today, done.

1313.title: Laudato Si' (2015)
1313.hook: Francis writes on care for our common home
1313.howItsDone: Catholic parishes and schools read Laudato Si' in study groups, some keep a Season of Creation in early autumn, and some form care-for-creation teams that work on energy, waste and local gardens.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Benedict's Caritas in Veritate, charity in truth. Your line was the logic of gift.

"Laudato si', mi' Signore." Praised be you, my Lord. That's a line from a song Francis of Assisi wrote, in his own Italian dialect, praising God through Brother Sun, Sister Moon, Brother Wind, Sister Water, and, as he puts it, our sister, Mother Earth. Centuries later, a pope who took Francis's name borrowed that line for the title of a letter. Not about prayer, exactly. About rivers, air, soil, the poor, and the way they're tied together. He addressed it not only to Catholics but to everyone living on the planet, with a subtitle: on care for our common home.
screen: `PRAISED BE YOU, MY LORD.` → `A SAINT'S SONG, A POPE'S LETTER.` → `OUR COMMON HOME.`

segments.voice: Francis calls the idea integral ecology. Integral means whole, nothing left out. First, the whole includes us. Ecology can sound like nature over there: forests, whales, glaciers. Francis says people are part of nature, included in it, not looking at it from outside, and what they do to it they do to themselves and to each other. Second, the crises are one crisis. There aren't two separate problems, one environmental and one social, but a single, complex crisis that is both. Polluted water and poverty, he says, often land on the same people. So caring for the earth and caring for the poor can't be split into separate departments. Third, the root is in the heart. He talks about habits: buying without thinking, using things up, rushing. He calls for an ecological conversion, a change of heart that shows up in small daily acts, like turning off unneeded lights, using less plastic, cooking only what will be eaten. Fourth, it starts in praise. Before it's a duty, it's wonder. This path met the verse back in year one, in the Douay-Rheims: "And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good." Very good, before anyone had used them for anything. Francis keeps returning to a phrase that sums it up, today's line: everything is connected. A choice at a grocery store, a factory far away, a family's water, a bird's nest, God's delight. One web.
screen: `PART OF NATURE, INCLUDED IN IT.` · `ONE CRISIS, BOTH SOCIAL AND NATURAL.` · `CONVERSION SHOWS IN SMALL HABITS.` · `IT STARTS IN PRAISE.` · then, large: `AND THEY WERE VERY GOOD.`

segments.voice: Go to a door or a window, or out onto a step; if you can't, close your eyes and remember the last time you stood outdoors. Notice one living thing, a tree, a weed in a crack, a bird, the sky itself, long enough to see something you missed, then follow one thread: the water it needs, the air you share with it. If you pray, say Francis of Assisi's line, praised be you, my Lord; if you don't, simply let yourself be glad it's there.
Integral ecology. The whole picture: the earth, the poor, our habits and our praise, held together as one. Today's word.
Your line: everything is connected. One web, and you're inside it. Until tomorrow.

1314.title: Two cries
1314.hook: hear both the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor
1314.howItsDone: Catholic groups that work on Laudato Si' often pair environmental projects with service to the poor, and some parishes and religious communities hold prayer services built around the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Laudato Si' and integral ecology. Your line was everything is connected.

A burning bush in the desert, and a voice from inside it. Moses, a shepherd on the run, hears God say, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have seen the affliction of my people in Egypt, and I have heard their cry." Before the plagues, before the sea, before any rescue, there's a God who listens. In Laudato Si', Pope Francis takes that act of hearing and doubles it. A true ecological approach, he says, must become a social approach, one that hears both the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor. Two cries. One pair of ears.
screen: `A VOICE FROM THE BUSH.` → `I HAVE HEARD THEIR CRY.` → `ONE PAIR OF EARS, TWO CRIES.`

segments.voice: First, the cry of the poor. A psalm in the Douay-Rheims puts it simply: "This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him." In the Catholic tradition, that cry has a claim on everyone who hears it. It's not background noise. Second, the cry of the earth. That sounds stranger. Can soil cry? Paul thinks creation itself has a voice. Writing to the Romans, he says: "For we know that every creature groaneth and travaileth in pain, even till now." Groaning, like a woman in labor. Francis picks up that language. He describes the earth as among the most abandoned and mistreated of the poor, burdened and laid waste. Third, why they belong together. When a forest is cleared, the families who lived from it are rarely the ones who profit from the timber. When land dries out, it's often the poorest farmers who can't move or adapt. So if you listen to only one cry, you'll mishear the other. An environmental plan that ignores the poor can end up pushing them aside. A plan for the poor that ignores the land can end up stripping what they live on. Fourth, hearing is the start. At the burning bush, God hears first, then acts. The order holds here too: listen, then respond. Not with despair, and not by trying to fix the whole world before lunch. With one real response, where you are.
screen: `THE CRY OF THE POOR.` · `THE CRY OF THE EARTH: CREATION GROANS.` · `HEAR ONE, AND YOU MISHEAR THE OTHER.` · `HEAR FIRST, THEN ACT.` · then, large: `EVERY CREATURE GROANETH AND TRAVAILETH.`

segments.voice: Let the cry of the poor come to mind, a person or a place you know is struggling, and stay with it a moment. Then let the cry of the earth come, a field paved over, a dirty creek, a summer that was too hot, and choose one of the two to answer with one small response: a donation, a call, a cleanup, a meal. If you pray, bring both cries to God; if you don't, simply let yourself hear them.
Two cries. The cry of the earth and the cry of the poor, which Francis says must be heard together. Today's word.
Your line: two cries. One pair of ears is enough to start. See you tomorrow.

1315.title: The throwaway culture
1315.hook: a culture that discards things and people
1315.carry: nothing and no one thrown away
1315.howItsDone: Catholics respond to Francis's critique of the throwaway culture in practical ways: parish repair cafés and food-rescue projects, visits to the elderly and the sick, and ministries that accompany people others overlook.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor. Your line was two cries.

A hillside by the Sea of Galilee. A huge crowd has just eaten, fed from five barley loaves and two fishes. Everyone is full. It's time to go home. But Jesus says to his disciples, in the Douay-Rheims: "Gather up the fragments that remain, lest they be lost." So they walk the hillside picking up leftovers, and the baskets fill. After a miracle of abundance, he cares about the scraps. Pope Francis has a name for the opposite habit, a way of living where whatever is no longer useful gets tossed.
screen: `A CROWD FED ON A HILLSIDE.` → `GATHER UP THE FRAGMENTS.` → `THE OPPOSITE HABIT.`

segments.voice: Francis calls it the throwaway culture. First, it starts with things. Phones replaced while they still work. Food bought and binned. Clothes worn twice. In Laudato Si', Francis points out that nature doesn't work like that: in a forest, what falls becomes food for something else. Human habits, he says, haven't learned that cycle, so waste piles up. Second, it doesn't stay with things. A culture that gets used to discarding objects slowly gets used to discarding people: whoever isn't productive, isn't convenient, isn't useful right now. Francis names who tends to be pushed out: the unborn, the elderly, the sick, the poor, migrants. In another letter, The Joy of the Gospel, he says the excluded are no longer even treated as exploited. They're treated as leftovers. Third, a different way of seeing. Every person, in Catholic teaching, has a dignity that doesn't depend on what they can do. The baby who can't work, the grandmother who can't remember, the man on the corner with a cardboard sign. Nobody is a leftover. That's why Francis keeps linking the earth and the person: the eyes that learn to see a broken chair as worth fixing can learn to see a slowed-down neighbor as worth visiting. Fourth, it's practiced in small things. Repair. Mend. Eat the leftovers. Visit the one nobody visits. These look like household tips. Francis treats them as a quiet protest against a whole way of life, an echo of the care on that hillside for crumbs.
screen: `IT STARTS WITH THINGS.` · `IT SPREADS TO PEOPLE.` · `NOBODY IS A LEFTOVER.` · `PRACTICED IN SMALL REPAIRS.` · then, large: `GATHER UP THE FRAGMENTS.`

segments.voice: Think of something at home that's broken or half-used and headed for the trash, a shirt with a loose button, a wobbly chair, food at the back of the fridge, and decide what fixing it, or using it up, would take. Then let your mind move from things to people: is there someone who has quietly been set aside, someone you haven't called because it's easier not to? If you pray, bring them to God; if you don't, just hold their name for a moment.
The throwaway culture. Francis's name for a way of living that discards things, and then people, once they stop being useful. Today's word.

1316.title: Fratelli Tutti (2020)
1316.hook: Francis retells the good Samaritan for a divided world
1316.howItsDone: Catholic parishes and schools study Fratelli Tutti, often alongside the parable of the good Samaritan, and some use it in interfaith gatherings and in ministries that visit people on the margins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the throwaway culture. Your line was nothing and no one thrown away.

Two words, Italian: fratelli tutti. All brothers. Francis of Assisi used them to address his brothers and sisters, the way someone might open a letter with dear friends. Pope Francis took them for the title of a letter about a world split into camps: nations against nations, neighbors who won't speak, strangers left on the side of the road. He didn't open his case with a theory. He sat down with a story Jesus told, about a man beaten and left half dead on the road to Jericho, and asked the reader a question. Which one of these people are you?
screen: `FRATELLI TUTTI: ALL BROTHERS.` → `A WORLD SPLIT INTO CAMPS.` → `WHICH ONE ARE YOU?`

segments.voice: First, the road, which this path first walked in year one. In Luke's Gospel, robbers strip a traveler and leave him by the road. A priest comes by and passes on the other side. A Levite does the same. Then a Samaritan, someone the listeners would have expected to keep his distance, stops, binds the wounds, and pays for the man's care at an inn. Second, the mirror. Francis says each of us can find ourselves in every character: sometimes the wounded man, sometimes the robbers, or the ones who pass by. He asks how often people look away, busy, sure it's someone else's job, and he notices that the passersby were religious men. Faith alone, in this story, doesn't make anyone stop. Third, the question flipped. A lawyer had asked Jesus, who is my neighbor? Jesus answers with the story, then turns the question around, in the Douay-Rheims: "Which of these three, in thy opinion, was neighbour to him that fell among the robbers?" The question isn't who counts as my neighbor. It's whether I'll become one. Fourth, the title. Jesus tells his disciples, "all you are brethren." Francis widens that circle to every person, across borders and parties and faiths. In the letter he writes of his conversations with a Muslim leader, the Grand Imam of al-Azhar, and of their shared call to fraternity. And the story ends with an instruction anyone can carry: "Go, and do thou in like manner." This week's thread, from the gospel of life to this road: no one is a stranger to be passed by.
screen: `A MAN LEFT ON THE ROAD TO JERICHO.` · `WE ARE EVERY CHARACTER.` · `NOT WHO IS MY NEIGHBOR, BUT BECOME ONE.` · `ALL YOU ARE BRETHREN.` · then, large: `GO, AND DO THOU IN LIKE MANNER.`

segments.voice: Picture a place you pass every day, a corner, a hallway, a parking lot, a group chat, and the person usually there on the edge whom you walk past, maybe not from unkindness, just from hurry. Imagine slowing down instead: a greeting, a question, five minutes. If you pray, ask God for the Samaritan's eyes; if you don't, simply hold the picture of yourself stopping.
Fratelli Tutti. All brothers: Francis's letter on fraternity, built around the good Samaritan. Today's word, and the end of this week.
Your line: all brothers and sisters. The road to Jericho runs past every door. That's the week.
